overview: One is your own immune system doing the work; the other is borrowed protection someone else's immune system already made.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Protection generated by the host's own immune system after exposure to an antigen (natural infection or vaccination).
aspects.valueB: Protection provided by antibodies transferred from another source, without the host's own immune system generating them.

aspects.label: Onset of Protection
aspects.valueA: Slower — takes days to weeks to develop full protection.
aspects.valueB: Immediate — protection is present as soon as the antibodies are transferred.

aspects.label: Duration of Protection
aspects.valueA: Long-lasting, often years to lifelong, due to immunological memory.
aspects.valueB: Short-lived, typically weeks to a few months, since no memory cells are generated.

aspects.label: Examples
aspects.valueA: Natural infection; vaccination with live-attenuated, inactivated, subunit, or mRNA vaccines.
aspects.valueB: Maternal antibodies crossing the placenta or in breast milk; immunoglobulin therapy (e.g. rabies or tetanus immunoglobulin).

aspects.label: Immunological Memory
aspects.valueA: Yes — memory B and T cells are generated.
aspects.valueB: No — no memory cells are generated in the recipient.

aspects.label: Typical Use Case
aspects.valueB: Post-exposure prophylaxis or protection for immunocompromised individuals needing immediate coverage.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueB: Externally provided, immediate onset, short duration.
